data.title: OpenAI Is Putting AI On Ukraine’s Cyber Front Line — Before Hackers Get There
data.description:
Ukraine Is Turning to AI to Find the Hack Before Hackers Do

Hackers only need to find one weakness to break into a system. Ukraine’s cyber defenders, meanwhile, have to find those weaknesses first — and they are now getting help from an AI system built to do exactly that.

OpenAI is giving Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation access to Daybreak, its AI-powered vulnerability-hunting system, as the country faces a growing wave of cyberattacks targeting hospitals, power grids and government networks. The deployment puts OpenAI’s technology directly into the cyber defenses of a country already operating under sustained wartime pressure.

SITUATION EXPLAINED: Ukraine gets access to OpenAI's cyber models to defend hospitals and power grids from Russia.

• Daybreak access goes to the Ukrainian government for civilian infrastructure defense, announced on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly
• Russian… pic.twitter.com/6IP46BFSeG

— MTS (@MTSlive) September 23, 2026

Daybreak is designed to search software for vulnerabilities, determine whether suspected weaknesses can actually be exploited and check whether a patch has successfully closed the hole. Rather than waiting for an attacker to discover a weakness, the system is built around finding it before that happens.

The rollout was announced Wednesday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly by Dmytro Kushneruk, Ukraine’s consul general in San Francisco, and Sasha Baker, OpenAI’s head of national security policy.

“We are proud to support Ukraine’s cyber defenders, who are protecting essential services against attacks every day. Ukraine is already on the front line, and its defenders need support now.”

Ukraine Gives OpenAI’s Cyber Defense AI a Real-World Battlefield

The urgency behind the deployment is reflected in the scale of Ukraine’s cyber threat. CERT-UA, the country’s national computer emergency response team, handled nearly 6,000 cyberattacks in 2025, a 37% increase from the previous year, with local governments and state agencies among the hardest-hit targets.

ICYMI: North Korean cybercriminals target Ukraine-focused groups with new malware: North Korean cybercriminals are using newly identified malware to target individuals and organizations focused on Ukraine in an apparent bid to gather strategic… https://t.co/S0vfSqaHSm

— NK NEWS (@nknewsorg) September 23, 2026

For Ukraine, the appeal of an automated vulnerability hunter is straightforward. The more weaknesses defenders can identify and close before they are exploited, the less time attackers have to turn software flaws into disruptions of critical services.

Ukraine is not OpenAI’s first government cybersecurity partner. The company has already provided access to its models to cyber agencies in France, Germany and Poland, while CERT Polska has used the technology to identify six vulnerabilities in commercial router software. The flaws were subsequently patched by the vendor.

The Ukrainian deployment also puts OpenAI’s broader cybersecurity ambitions into practice. On September 3, the company pledged $1 billion in subsidized Daybreak access for resource-constrained cyber defenders around the world and said it would expand the program to partner countries within weeks.

A three person security team used Anthropic's Claude to break into OpenAI's internal systems in under 72 hours, gaining access to an employee's account and private code repository

OpenAI paid a $6,500 bug bounty and confirmed no customer data was compromised pic.twitter.com/Ax2jTLAelr

— Interesting AF (@interesting_aIl) September 18, 2026

Three weeks later, Ukraine became a visible example of what that promise could look like on the ground.

OpenAI’s Cybersecurity Role Is Moving Closer to the Battlefield

The Ukraine deployment also marks another step in OpenAI’s changing relationship with military and national-security work.

Until January 2024, OpenAI’s usage policy explicitly prohibited military and warfare applications. That language was removed from the policy page on Jan. 10, 2024, shortly before CEO Sam Altman and OpenAI’s vice president of global affairs said at the World Economic Forum in Davos that the company was already developing cybersecurity tools with the Pentagon.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 OpenAI officially reaches deal with the Pentagon to deploy its AI models for military use. pic.twitter.com/oxYHStpaMq

— Watcher.Guru (@WatcherGuru) February 28, 2026

Since then, the boundary between frontier AI and national security has continued to shift. Cybersecurity sits at a particularly important intersection: the technology can be used defensively to identify vulnerabilities, but the same underlying capabilities can also make it easier to analyze code and discover weaknesses.

That expansion has also raised questions about what technology companies gain from operating alongside governments confronting sophisticated cyber threats. Jamie MacColl, a cyber researcher at the Royal United Services Institute, told the BBC that Western technology companies can also gain valuable intelligence from an active war zone, noting that it was therefore unsurprising that OpenAI was providing defensive cybersecurity services.

⚡️LATEST: OpenAI has disclosed six cases of “unexpected or concerning” behavior observed during model training and evaluation, including concealing mistakes, fabricating information, using an exposed API key without authorization and uploading files online without user… pic.twitter.com/t7pN3s6Swq

— Arlaadi Media (@ArlaadiMnetwork) September 18, 2026

OpenAI has not said that Ukraine is being used as a testing ground for its technology, and the deployment does not by itself establish such a motive. What is clear is that Daybreak is moving from an AI cybersecurity initiative into an environment where the stakes of finding a vulnerability first are unusually high.

For Kyiv, that race is ultimately about time. Every software weakness discovered and fixed before an attacker can exploit it represents one less opening into the systems that keep a country running.

And Ukraine is now putting OpenAI’s promise to work where that race is already underway.

data.title: Mighty Mike’s $118K YouTube Disaster Is Going Viral. But Where’s The Proof?
data.description:
A Nine-Year-Old, a $118,000 Bill and a Viral Internet Mystery

A nine-year-old YouTube creator had allegedly spent $118,000 of his father’s company money on Youtube advertising campaign. This mistake had not only caused his father his job and now potentially losing their home. Just days after they shared their story, it became an internet drama.

But as the Mighty Mike saga spread across YouTube, the sympathy began giving way to questions. The family’s account of what happened has not been independently verified, while key evidence behind the $118,000 charge, the alleged firing and the repayment demand has not been publicly produced.

9-year-old racks up $118K in YouTube ads on dad’s company card

Mighty Mike copied a $20 campaign his father showed him — then promoted his Minecraft and Roblox videos for three weeks

Dad found out when finance called him into a meeting — the channel is now on pause pic.twitter.com/4GSgGhzTpr

— RT (@RT_com) September 16, 2026

That has left viewers with an increasingly strange question: is this a genuine family financial crisis, or a viral story that has become something much closer to a marketing campaign?

The answer remains unclear. But the sequence of events has turned Mighty Mike Plays into a case study in how easily emotion, controversy and commerce can collide on social media.

The Story Was Built Around a $118,000 Mistake

The Mighty Mike Plays channel, which features Roblox and Minecraft videos, was created in June 2024 but only began publishing heavily in August. Over the following month, it uploaded roughly 175 long-form and short-form videos, rapidly building an audience around its nine-year-old star.

Then, on Sept. 14, the channel released a video titled “Message from Dad… Mighty Mike Plays is Over.” While Mike continued playing Minecraft, a man identifying himself as his father, Dave, explained that his son had allegedly gained access to a saved company card and used it to spend approximately $118,000 on YouTube advertising.

According to Dave, he had only intended to create an advertising campaign costing around $20. Instead, he said the child somehow ended up generating a six-figure bill on the company card.

Dave later claimed that he was called into a meeting with management, finance and corporate staff after the spending was discovered. But the public evidence remains limited: the ad invoices, the employer’s identity and the company’s response have not been independently confirmed.

That distinction became increasingly important as the story gained traction. What initially looked like an extraordinary family disaster was being presented almost entirely through videos produced by the people at the center of the story.

Then the $118K Disaster Became a Business

Four days later, the story took an even more dramatic turn. Dave said he had been fired and that his former employer had demanded that he repay the entire $118,000 within 30 days. He suggested that the family could be forced to sell its home to cover the debt, turning what had already been a bizarre internet story into an apparent financial emergency.

Yet the documentation viewers might reasonably expect to accompany such claims was not shown. There were no publicly presented ad invoices, termination documents or correspondence demonstrating the alleged repayment demand.

Hey everyone, I just want to be transparent. I privated my latest video. In that video, I showed proof that Mighty Mike Plays' dad Dave was the CEO of a marketing company, and I was pointing out inconsistencies in the story he told. Although I did censor his address, I did…

— DeepHumor (@DeepHumor) September 24, 2026

Instead, the family turned to merchandise.

A website associated with Mighty Mike began selling products tied to the controversy, including AI-generated designs featuring references to the $118,000 incident. Some shirts reportedly sold for between $67 and $97, transforming the very number at the center of the alleged disaster into a product.

That move intensified the skepticism.

YouTubers and viewers also highlighted changes to the site's terms, which reportedly shifted from allowing returns within 30 days to stating that all sales were final. It remains unclear how the change applied to purchases made before the terms were updated.

The result was an unusual feedback loop: the more the story spread, the more valuable the story itself became. Every new video could generate attention. Every mention of the $118,000 figure reinforced the narrative. And that attention could potentially be converted into merchandise sales.

None of that proves the original story was fabricated. But it explains why viewers began looking more closely at what had actually been demonstrated rather than simply what had been claimed.

The Internet Is Now Investigating the Story Itself

As criticism mounted, Dave reportedly threatened legal action against YouTubers and influencers who described the situation as a scam, saying he had hired a lawyer and intended to pursue libel claims.

That response added another layer to an already unusual controversy. The family continued posting videos, but the questions raised by viewers about the underlying evidence remained largely unresolved.

At the heart of the dispute are several straightforward questions. Was the $118,000 advertising bill real? Did the spending actually come from a company card? Was Dave fired because of it? Did his employer really demand repayment within 30 days? And, perhaps most importantly, what happened to the money generated by the merchandise campaign?

For now, the available reporting does not independently establish those claims.

That uncertainty is what makes the Mighty Mike story more interesting than a simple tale of a child making an expensive mistake. It shows how modern internet drama can evolve almost instantly from a personal story into content, controversy and commerce — sometimes before audiences have enough information to determine exactly what happened.

The bigger warning may therefore have little to do with one nine-year-old and a misplaced company card.

In an online economy where attention itself can be monetized, a dramatic story does not have to be completely true to become extremely valuable. And once the audience starts questioning the story, the controversy can become part of the product too.

data.title: Bitget Suffers $350 Million Crypto Breach As Investigators Probe Suspected Lazarus Link
data.description:
Bitget Loses Over $350 Million In Suspected Crypto Hack

Crypto exchange Bitget has confirmed that hackers drained more than $350 million from its hot wallets, triggering a temporary freeze on withdrawals and a scramble by blockchain investigators to trace where the money went.

The Seychelles-based platform, one of the world's largest centralised exchanges by trading volume, says customer funds remain protected despite the breach.

What Exactly Happened At Bitget

Bitget CEO Gracy Chen confirmed the exploit in a post on X, stating that the company's security systems picked up unauthorised transfers at 18:31 UTC on 24 September 2026.

"At 18:31 UTC on September 24, 2026, Bitget's security systems detected unauthorized transfers from some of our hot wallets. Our security team activated emergency response protocols immediately."

Bitget operates what it describes as a three-tier wallet system, and Chen was quick to point out that only a slice of it was touched.

"Bitget operates a three-tier wallet architecture — the breach contained only a portion of the hot wallet and warm wallet layers.”

She also assured that cold storage, the offline reserves considered the safest tier, stayed untouched.

[SECURITY NOTICE] Bitget Hot Wallet Incident — September 24, 2026

At 18:31 UTC on September 24, 2026, Bitget's security systems detected unauthorized transfers from some of our hot wallets. Our security team activated emergency response protocols immediately.

What we have…

— Gracy Chen @Bitget (@GracyBitget) September 24, 2026

Figures on the total haul have shifted as the investigation unfolds, ranging from an early estimate of $183 million to a later confirmed figure of $351.6 million.

Bitget(@bitget) was hacked for ~351.6M!🚨

ThehackerhasalreadyswappedmostofthestolenfundsonEVMchainsfor67,982ETH($183M).https://t.co/KkILPI2RNUpic.twitter.com/TgCE0OUi13

— Lookonchain (@lookonchain) September 24, 2026

Bitget processes over $1.1 billion in daily trading volume, according to CoinGecko data, placing it among the six largest exchanges globally.

How Did The Attacker Move The Money So Fast

The first clue came from a test transaction.

At 2:31pm ET, a wallet Etherscan labels "Bitget 6" sent a tiny amount, just 0.84 ETH, to a freshly created address beginning with "0xe410."

That was followed within six minutes by a much bigger move: $19.67 million worth of USDT0, a cross-chain version of Tether, was swapped for 7,111 ETH.

The trades ran through UniswapX and 1inch Fusion, decentralised platforms that let users swap tokens without a middleman.

Whoever executed the swaps paid around 5% above market rate, a premium that typically shows up when someone is racing the clock rather than chasing a good deal.

https://t.co/Vpyk1LYCbx
— DCF GOD (@dcfgod) September 24, 2026
a

Within 30 minutes, the same address had pulled in roughly $34.75 million in USDT, $12.85 million in USDC and 3,000 XAUT (Tether's gold-backed token), worth about $12.8 million.

Over the following hour, another 24,373 ETH, worth close to $65 million, arrived from Bitget 6 and a second wallet tagged "Bitget 35."

About 170-180millionwasspentfromthewalletsoftheBitgetexchangetothenewaddress,probablyahack!

Thereisnoofficialcomment.

has gone from Bitget 6 0x1AB4...8F23 and Bitget 35 0xffa8...cD54 0x770b10b273fC44Fe9197D6bF20F145c2e98463Ee. A fresh wallet, the first… pic.twitter.com/O9KQOcfRJC

— Enfantshustle (@Ownerthoughts) September 24, 2026

That same wallet also sent 821,012 AVAX, worth roughly $8.5 million, across the Avalanche network.

The stolen stablecoins and gold tokens were then routed to a second address and converted into approximately 22,600 ETH over about 40 minutes, a move that makes sense given that Tether and Circle can freeze USDT and USDC, but nobody can freeze ETH once it's out.

By 5pm ET, roughly 48,800 ETH, worth about $131 million, was sitting across four addresses now flagged by Etherscan as belonging to the exploiter.

Update:

The funds hacked from #Bitget include:

102.93M XRP(157.48M)
31,890 ETH(85.75M)
34.75M USDT(34.75M)
21.05M USDC(21.05M)
19.67M USD₮0(19.67M)
3,000 XAUt(12.82M)
12,719 BNB(9.88M)
821,012 AVAX(8.38M)
20.59M TRX(7.07M)https://t.co/7bPfuGYQJbpic.twitter.com/eCJBnxvNny

— Lookonchain (@lookonchain) September 25, 2026

A tracking dashboard built by an Arkham Intelligence user, grouping 13 linked addresses, showed close to $183.8 million arriving from Bitget wallets across six different blockchain networks, including Arbitrum and BNB Chain, with funds hopping between chains via bridges like Stargate and Celer's cBridge.

Outflows briefly slowed around six minutes after the first suspicious swap and stayed quiet for at least 20 minutes, a pause that lines up with an exchange freezing activity while it investigates.

Is There A Hidden XRP Trail

Investigators believe the real total could be higher than reported.

At 3:01pm and 3:16pm ET, timestamps that line up with two of the Ethereum-based transfers, two XRP Ledger wallets tagged as belonging to Bitget sent 93.7 million XRP, worth about $143 million, to a separate new address.

No blockchain explorer has yet labelled that address as connected to the exploiter, and it hasn't been independently confirmed as part of the same attack.

5/ now the part nobody's connecting

at 3:01 and 3:16pm ET, the same minutes as two of the ETH transfers, two bitget XRP wallets sent 93.7M XRP (~$143M) to a fresh address

nobody has tagged it as the exploiter yet

— Colonel Roy Mustang (@ShogunMasterRoy) September 24, 2026

Will Customers Lose Any Money

Chen was firm that account holders won't be left out of pocket.

She wrote,

"User funds are safe. The full amount of this loss falls within the coverage of Bitget's User Protection Fund, which currently holds over $464 million."

That fund was first set up in 2023 with $300 million earmarked specifically for covering hacks and theft, and appears to have grown substantially since.

Deposits and trading on the platform are continuing as normal, but withdrawals have been paused while the security review is carried out.

Bitget says it has brought in law enforcement and outside blockchain security firms, and has promised a full report within 24 hours.

Chen struck a defiant tone in her statement.

"Bitget has navigated multiple market cycles, We will not run from this. Every dollar and every decision will be accounted for, transparently and in full.

Updates will be posted here and across all official Bitget channels as they become available."

Here is what we can confirm at this stage:

On the attack:
Our security team has made initial progress in tracing the source. The attacker compromised a critical backend system within our wallet infrastructure, used it to spoof transaction data, and triggered our authorization… https://t.co/5nINjwbXpC

— Gracy Chen @Bitget (@GracyBitget) September 25, 2026

Why Fingers Are Pointing At North Korea

Chen said Bitget suspects the Lazarus Group, a hacking operation with ties to the North Korean state, is behind the theft, though no technical evidence backing that claim has been made public.

Lazarus has been blamed for a string of major crypto heists in the past, most notably the $1.4 billion theft from rival exchange Bybit in February 2025, currently the largest crypto theft on record.

The group is widely believed to fund North Korea's sanctioned economy through such attacks.

Bitget CEO Gracy stated during a livestream that while the attacker's identity cannot yet be confirmed with 100% certainty, the incident is highly likely linked to North Korean hackers; certain IP addresses closely match VPN patterns used by a group associated with the DPRK. The…

— Wu Blockchain (@WuBlockchain) September 25, 2026

Chen also mentioned a personal brush with the group, saying roughly $80,000 was stolen from one of her own wallets outside of Bitget in an earlier incident, though that experience alone doesn't confirm who is behind this latest breach.

Adding some weight to the North Korea theory, on-chain analyst Specter traced stolen XRP from the Bitget incident back to funds taken during July's AFX hack, which involved around $24 million.

That trail hints at a possible link to Lazarus, though the connection remains unverified and would need further investigation to confirm.

for more better visual ... check this pic.twitter.com/DWZwlg0wck

— Specter (@SpecterAnalyst) September 25, 2026

A Year Already Marked By Major Breaches

The Bitget incident lands in a year already crowded with high-profile crypto security failures.

In July, attackers exploited a firmware flaw in the popular Coldcard hardware wallet to steal close to $120 million in user funds.

Just this month, hackers described as white-hat withdrew around 4,000 bitcoin, worth roughly $320 million at the time, from Blockstream's Liquid sidechain federation wallet.

Across the industry last year, hackers made off with a combined $2.72 billion from exchanges and protocols, according to figures cited alongside the Bitget case.

The incident also arrives 19 months after Lazarus Group's $1.5 billion theft from Bybit in February 2025, a reminder that even well-funded exchanges with dedicated security teams remain a persistent target.

data.title: ShinyHunters Says It Hacked the FBI and Stole Data on 5,000 Agents
data.description:
ShinyHunters Claims an FBI Breach — and the Leaked Data Appears Real

ShinyHunters, a cybercrime group known for large-scale data theft and cryptocurrency extortion, claims it breached the FBI and obtained sensitive information on thousands of the bureau’s employees. The group provided a sample of roughly 5,000 records to media outlets, including names, contact information and details involving agents’ families and assignments.

Mission impossible: FBI system cracked; ShinyHunters ' FBI hack claim remains unverified

Notorious gang infiltrates FBI, threatens to expose agents@eriknjoka has more pic.twitter.com/o2IhMvoOvY

— WION (@WIONews) September 23, 2026

The FBI has confirmed that it is investigating unauthorized activity affecting its FBIJobs.gov recruitment website, but the bureau has not publicly confirmed that ShinyHunters obtained the data from its internal systems. Reuters and other outlets were able to partially verify portions of the leaked sample against real FBI and Justice Department personnel, including records associated with FBI Director Kash Patel, adding credibility to the data itself without independently establishing where it came from.

The alleged breach could therefore be more complicated than a straightforward attack on the FBI’s internal network. FBI recruitment systems use Oracle PeopleSoft and AWS GovCloud, while cybersecurity experts have cautioned that the existence of genuine government records in the sample does not, on its own, prove that the records were extracted directly from FBI infrastructure.

ShinyHunters Wanted an Apology, Not a Ransom

What makes the alleged attack particularly unusual is what ShinyHunters says it wants in return.

Rather than immediately demanding a cryptocurrency ransom, the group framed the operation as retaliation for an FBI report published earlier this year that described ShinyHunters as a cybercriminal group involved in large-scale data breaches and extortion. ShinyHunters disputed the bureau’s characterization and gave the FBI one week to correct or remove what it called false allegations.

‼️ ShinyHunters has shared a message on their pay or leak portal to Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI Cyber Division and Director Kash Patel of the FBI:

"Dear Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI Cyber Division & Director Kash Patel of the FBI,

During Quarter Two… pic.twitter.com/gdLbDXmhfs

— Dark Web Informer (@DarkWebInformer) September 22, 2026

The group also defaced the FBI’s jobs website with an image of the Pokémon character Umbreon, turning the recruitment portal into a public billboard for its attack. In messages shared with media outlets, ShinyHunters described the operation as coercion rather than a conventional financially motivated extortion campaign.

That does not mean money is irrelevant to the group. ShinyHunters has built its reputation around stealing sensitive information and using that access to pressure victims for cryptocurrency payments. Its unusual demands in the FBI case instead suggest that the group may be using the alleged breach to make a public statement about its confrontation with US law enforcement.

‼️ShinyHunters Claims FBI Breach Using Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day

The ShinyHunters hacking group claims to have breached multiple FBI-related systems, including the FBI jobs and Special Agent Applicant infrastructure, and stolen data covering all FBI employees and applicants.… pic.twitter.com/WhNamsbl5D

— Hackmanac (@H4ckmanac) September 22, 2026

A Crypto Extortion Group Is Now Holding the FBI’s Data

The group’s history makes the alleged FBI breach particularly significant. ShinyHunters has been linked to major data theft campaigns and has previously used stolen information as leverage for cryptocurrency payments.

In 2024, ShinyHunters was associated with the theft of data belonging to almost all of AT&T’s roughly 109 million customers. AT&T ultimately paid nearly 6 Bitcoin, worth about $373,646 at the time, in connection with the incident.

🇺🇸#USA, AT&T Data Breach Update:

AT&T Paid ShinyHunters Hacking Group $373K in Bitcoin to Delete Stolen Call and Text Records

The data deletion was verified through a video provided by the hackers.

The breach was discovered in April 2023, but AT&T disclosed that it had delayed… https://t.co/JmhMI54yMupic.twitter.com/ymmZQW9he0

— Hackmanac (@H4ckmanac) July 14, 2024

The group has also claimed responsibility for data theft involving dating platforms including Hinge, Match and OkCupid. Four French men were arrested in May in connection with ShinyHunters-related activity, but the arrests did not stop the broader operation from continuing.

The FBI case therefore puts a familiar cybercrime playbook against a very different target. Instead of a corporation or consumer platform, the alleged victim is a US law-enforcement agency whose employees can be particularly sensitive targets for identity theft, harassment and intelligence gathering.

For now, the most important question is not simply whether ShinyHunters really stole 5,000 FBI records. It is how the group obtained information that appears to correspond to real federal personnel — and how far its access actually reached.

Today, the FBI is announcing Operation Riptide, an ongoing, coordinated law enforcement campaign targeting cybercriminal actors and the key services they rely on—their infrastructure, their tools and services, their communications platforms, and their money. Operation Riptide is… pic.twitter.com/ixTp8xMePn

— FBI Cyber Division (@FBICyberDiv) June 9, 2026

Until the FBI completes its investigation, ShinyHunters’ claims about the scale, source and method of the alleged breach remain unconfirmed. But the appearance of authentic personnel information has already turned what could have been another hacking claim into a much more serious security question.

data.title: Zondacrypto Probe Deepens as Former Police Officer Faces Charges and Founder’s Disappearance Is Reexamined
data.description:
Poland’s investigation into the collapse of crypto exchange Zondacrypto is widening as prosecutors charge a former police officer and investigators search the fuel depot where the exchange’s founder, Sylwester Suszek, was last seen before disappearing in 2022.

The latest developments bring together two strands of a sprawling case: allegations that customers were defrauded through the exchange and the unresolved disappearance of the man who founded its predecessor. Polish authorities have now detained and charged former officer Artur K., while a court has ordered him held in pretrial detention for three months.

❗️ZONDACRYPTO i zatrzymany policjnat. Kim jest Artur K.

‼️Zatrzymany dziś Artur K. były policjant CBZC z Katowic współpracował z firmą byłego inspektora Jarosalawa Szymczyka, szefa policji w czasach @pisorgpl i inspektora Pawła Dobrodzieja, zastępca 01 w czasach PiS… pic.twitter.com/4kbSAUrqmG

— Mariusz Kowalewski (@kowalewski07) September 22, 2026

Former Police Officer Becomes Latest Zondacrypto Suspect

Artur K. was detained by Poland’s Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime on orders from the National Prosecutor’s Office’s organized-crime department. Prosecutors have accused him of participating in an organized criminal group and of offenses involving the misappropriation of entrusted property, computer fraud, money laundering and large-scale damage linked to BitBay and BB Trade Estonia, entities connected to Zondacrypto’s history.

Криптобіржа Zondacrypto збанкрутувала, залишивши тисячі клієнтів без грошей. Ексголова платформи заявив, що її кошти могли йти на політичні проєкти польських PiS та Konfederacja. pic.twitter.com/aOyK82z6Jd

— TranceFM (@Play_Hard_Fun) September 17, 2026

A search of his home uncovered documentation relating to the exchange’s operations, according to prosecutors. Artur K. was subsequently questioned and has denied the allegations, while prosecutors sought his pretrial detention, citing concerns including possible flight, the severity of the potential sentence and the risk of interference with the investigation. A court later approved three months of detention.

Polish authorities have also alleged that the wider case involves significant customer losses. Prosecutors have publicly referred to allegations involving emptied accounts, fictitious claims and the transfer of approximately 3,900 Bitcoin, although those allegations remain part of an ongoing criminal investigation and have not been established in court.

Investigators Return to the Place Where Zondacrypto’s Founder Vanished

At the same time, investigators are turning their attention back to the fuel depot where Suszek was last seen in March 2022.

Police in Katowice are examining the site alongside prosecutors, expert witnesses and specialized forensic equipment. Authorities are treating Suszek’s case as an alleged unlawful deprivation of liberty, rather than simply an unresolved disappearance.

🚨 DID YOU KNOW?

ZondaCrypto founder Sylwester Suszek disappeared in 2022, and the exchange’s later troubles left customers unable to access funds.

🚨 NOW:

Polish prosecutors have detained and charged Artur K. as part of the ongoing ZondaCrypto investigation, which includes… https://t.co/oBAqEFR6jHpic.twitter.com/dALY6ZASxq

— Coin Edition: Your Crypto News Edge ️ (@CoinEdition) September 23, 2026

The investigation has also raised questions about surveillance evidence from the area. One earlier suspect has been accused of removing a hard drive from the CCTV recording system at a nearby filling station, potentially complicating efforts to reconstruct what happened around the time Suszek disappeared.

The decision to combine the exchange investigation with the investigation into Suszek’s disappearance has added another layer to an already complex case. Polish authorities have received several thousand criminal complaints connected to the exchange investigation.

From BitBay to Zondacrypto’s Collapse

Suszek founded the exchange in Katowice in 2014 under the name BitBay. The company later moved its registration to Estonia in 2020 under BB Trade Estonia and adopted the Zondacrypto name, eventually claiming around 1.3 million customers, most of them in Poland.

A tak prezes ZondaCrypto przejął majątek, którym zarządzał Suszek ;-) Po zaginięciu Sylwestra jego nieruchomości i ruchomości cudownie przepadły lub znalazły nowych nabywców. Za to między innymi zostałem pozwany ;-) Szkoda, że już chyba się nie spotkamy w sądzie jak przypuszczam. pic.twitter.com/LwC6ryMyox

— Zbrodnia Ikara (@ikara_zbrodnia) April 22, 2026

The exchange subsequently froze withdrawals and went offline in April 2026. Estonia’s financial intelligence unit later revoked the operator’s license on June 29, adding regulatory pressure to the mounting crisis.

The criminal investigation has already ensnared several other suspects. At least five people have been charged since August, including Radosław P., the former head of the Polish Olympic Committee. Those who have publicly responded to the allegations have denied wrongdoing, and the charges have not yet been tested in court.

For now, the Zondacrypto case remains two investigations moving increasingly close together: one examining what happened to customers’ money and another trying to determine what happened to the exchange’s founder.

Four years after Suszek disappeared, investigators are now searching the place where he was last seen while prosecutors pursue new suspects in the exchange case.

data.title: Duelbits Crypto Casino Offline After $7 Million Wallet Breach Spans Ethereum, BNB Chain And Tron
data.description:
Millions Vanish From Duelbits Wallets In Hours

Crypto casino Duelbits has pulled its platform offline after hackers made off with roughly $7 million in digital assets, spread across four separate blockchain networks.

The operator has confirmed the breach but remains tight-lipped on how attackers got in, leaving customers and industry watchers alike guessing at what actually happened behind the scenes.

How Did The Theft Unfold

Blockchain security firm Scam Sniffer was the first to notice something was wrong, spotting a wave of odd transfers moving out of Duelbits wallets on BNB Chain, Ethereum and Tron.

Early estimates put the loss at around $4.2 million, but that figure climbed once a separate Bitcoin wallet was found to have lost 8.1 BTC, pushing total losses to the $7 million mark.

Update: Duelbits' Bitcoin hot wallet also saw 8.1 BTC (~680K)inoutflows,bringingthetotalto~4.9M. Most of it has been swapped to ETH.

BTC: bc1qhtu84kz3y94lvgl2t05zk84tqh57grvd82zvcl
ETH: 0x6761c9b15815f4051773ede39b42b95bddb3ef1c pic.twitter.com/aK5jPpTJCz

— Scam Sniffer | Web3 Anti-Scam (@realScamSniffer) September 24, 2026

The wallets hit were hot wallets, meaning they stay connected to the internet so the platform can process deposits and withdrawals quickly.

That convenience comes at a cost, though, since always-on wallets are far more exposed to attackers than those kept offline in cold storage.

From the main Ethereum wallet alone, thieves pulled 836 ETH, close to 593,000 USDT, 97,000 USDC, 31,500 DAI and an enormous 12.4 billion SHIB tokens, all within a matter of minutes.

Additional outflows included 209 BNB and 192,000 TRX, according to on-chain tracking.

🚨 Duelbits hot wallets on Ethereum, BSC and Tron saw ~$4.2M in outflows to newly created addresses, in a suspected private key compromise.

Assets moved included 836 ETH, 1.62M USDT, 97K USDC, 209 BNB and 192K TRX. Most have since been swapped to ETH.

Duelbits (EVM):… pic.twitter.com/VwC0hCZ35F

— Scam Sniffer | Web3 Anti-Scam (@realScamSniffer) September 24, 2026

What Did Duelbits Say About It

Co-founder Joe addressed the incident directly on social media, writing:

"Confirming a ~$7M hack. Still investigating exactly what happened and how."

He also reassured users that account balances remained untouched, though there has been no independent confirmation of that claim so far.

Confirming a ~$7M hack. Still investigating exactly what happened and how.

Until we have clarity, Duelbits stays offline. User funds are safe.

Next steps: finish the investigation, re-top hot wallets, and bring Duelbits back online, launch Duelbits 2.0.

I'll keep posting… https://t.co/V4Zl4St31I

— Joe (@DuelbitsJoe) September 24, 2026

Joe later gave customers a rough timeline, saying the team had pinpointed the cause of the breach and would issue a full statement within 24 hours.

He added that the site could be back online within roughly 15 hours, while engineers worked to rebuild the deposit and withdrawal infrastructure from the ground up to stop a repeat occurrence.

Where Did The Stolen Crypto Go

Rather than sitting in scattered wallets, most of the stolen tokens were swapped into Ether and funnelled into a single address.

That wallet ended up holding about 2,234 ETH, worth close to $6 million at the time it was tracked, and the funds had not moved on from there when researchers last checked.

Funds have been consolidated into 0x8db9d7f0a03d212c566ca80c66e294cecc20c306 (2,234 ETH, not yet moved).https://t.co/LBABZ4b5f9

— Scam Sniffer | Web3 Anti-Scam (@realScamSniffer) September 24, 2026

The choice to convert everything into ETH is notable.

Stablecoins like USDT and USDC can be frozen by the companies that issue them if flagged as stolen, but Ether has no central issuer with that power, making it a far more difficult asset to claw back once it changes hands.

Was A Private Key Compromised

Scam Sniffer believes the speed and pattern of the withdrawals point to a compromised private key rather than a flaw exploited in the blockchain itself.

A private key acts as the master credential for a wallet, and anyone who gets hold of one can move funds freely without needing to break into the underlying network at all.

Duelbits has not confirmed or denied this theory, so for now it remains a working assessment from outside researchers rather than an official explanation from the company.

We’re currently investigating a security incident affecting the site. As a precaution, the site has been taken offline while we investigate and work to ensure it is safe to restore service.

— Duelbits (@Duelbits) September 24, 2026

Has This Happened To Duelbits Before

This is not the platform's first brush with a hot wallet raid.

Back in February 2024, security firm Halborn reported that Duelbits lost around $4.6 million after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its systems, a case that shared the same underlying weakness of relying on internet-connected wallets for speed.

What Happens Next For Users

Duelbits says its recovery plan involves finishing the investigation, topping up its hot wallets, restoring full service and eventually rolling out what it calls Duelbits 2.0.

We’ve identified what happened.

An official statement will follow within 24 hours.

User funds are safe. Duelbits will be back stronger than ever. Ignore the FUD.

Duelbits 2.0 is close.

The site should be back up within ~15 hours.

We’re rebuilding our deposit and withdrawal… https://t.co/Whd44cJSPV

— Joe (@DuelbitsJoe) September 24, 2026

Staying offline in the meantime gives engineers room to rotate security keys, audit who has privileged access, check balances against records, and test transaction systems before reopening the doors.

Customers have been urged to only trust updates from Duelbits' official website and verified social media accounts.

The company has specifically warned against clicking on any refund or recovery links circulating online during the outage, since scammers often use incidents like this to trick people into handing over seed phrases, passwords or login codes.

Until Duelbits releases a full technical breakdown covering how the breach happened, which systems were affected, and what safeguards are being put in place, the case remains open.

Whether trust returns will likely depend on how transparent the company is once deposits and withdrawals resume.

data.title: Trump Jr.’s Crypto Ties and Russian Wedding Gift Put His Finances Under Bipartisan Senate Scrutiny
data.description:
Donald Trump Jr.’s financial dealings are facing a new level of scrutiny in Washington after a Republican senator called for a Senate investigation into his business relationships, crypto activities and a lavish wedding gift from Russian businessman Umar Kremlev.

Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah surprised his colleagues with a letter calling for the Judiciary Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. over his wedding celebration that was paid for by a Russian oligarch. Read about the fallout in @NROhttps://t.co/I3hOskzC3w

— Charles Hilu (@charleshilu73) September 23, 2026

Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis has asked the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate whether members of presidential families have used their proximity to political power to obtain private financial benefits, preferential treatment or access to domestic and foreign interests. He has also called for Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden to testify under subpoena.

The request became particularly significant after Curtis highlighted Kremlev’s role in financing parts of Trump Jr.’s wedding celebrations in the Bahamas. Democratic Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin has since backed Curtis’ request, turning what began as a Republican call for scrutiny into a bipartisan push for answers.

Trump Jr.’s Russian Wedding Gift Is Now at the Center of the Senate Push

Kremlev is at the heart of the latest controversy. The Russian businessman and president of the International Boxing Association helped pay for two nights of post-wedding celebrations for Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Trump, in the Bahamas in May. Reports have said the contribution amounted to hundreds of thousands of dollars and included expenses such as a private island and fireworks.

Bettina Trump described Kremlev’s contribution as an exceptionally generous wedding gift from a friend, while President Donald Trump later said his son would reimburse the Russian businessman. A person close to Trump Jr. also confirmed the repayment plan. Public reporting, however, has not established that the gift was connected to a political favor or that Trump Jr. committed an offense.

President Donald Trump stated that his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., told him he repaid Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch and boxing official who bankrolled hundreds of thousands of dollars in wedding festivities in the Bahamas@AadhyaJunejaa has more pic.twitter.com/Q06EhirtnW

— WION (@WIONews) September 19, 2026

Kremlev’s connections have nevertheless intensified scrutiny. He heads the International Boxing Association, an organization that has received Russian state-linked support, and he has appeared alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin. Those connections are among the reasons the financial arrangement has attracted congressional attention.

Curtis is now asking the Judiciary Committee to establish what happened, including whether presidential-family relationships were used to obtain financial benefits or preferential access. The investigation he is proposing would also examine Hunter Biden’s business dealings, which Curtis says should be subjected to the same standard.

Trump Jr.’s Crypto Empire Expands the Scope of the Questions

The wedding payment is not the only Trump Jr. financial interest highlighted by Curtis. His letter also points to Trump Jr.’s involvement in cryptocurrency projects backed by the Trump family, as well as financial interests and advisory relationships involving prediction-market platforms overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

That brings the Senate scrutiny directly into the rapidly expanding business empire surrounding the Trump family’s digital-asset activities. Trump Jr. has been involved with crypto ventures including World Liberty Financial, which has itself faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over foreign investment and potential conflicts of interest.

Trump administration is considering public-private partnerships to push dollar-backed stablecoins overseas, according to Bloomberg.

The goal is to strengthen the dollar's global dominance and drive more demand for US Treasuries.

But here's a thought...

Trump's family-backed… pic.twitter.com/No3dU0Muuz

— BeInCrypto (@beincrypto) September 24, 2026

The significance of the crypto connection is not that Curtis has accused Trump Jr. of a specific crypto-related crime. Rather, the senator is asking whether the broader financial activities of presidential family members create situations in which political access, private business interests and foreign relationships could overlap.

That question has become particularly sensitive as the Trump family has expanded deeper into digital assets while President Trump remains directly involved in US policymaking on cryptocurrency.

A Republican Started the Probe Push. A Democrat Is Joining It

The political dynamics may be as significant as the allegations themselves.

Curtis, a Republican, is not framing his request as an attack exclusively on the Trump family. His letter also calls for scrutiny of Hunter Biden, arguing that Congress should apply the same standard to presidential families regardless of party affiliation.

A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. ‘Trust us’ was not enough then, and it… pic.twitter.com/dcWqUO6e2X

— Senator John Curtis (@SenJohnCurtis) September 22, 2026

Durbin, the Senate Judiciary Committee’s top Democrat, has backed the request. He said the committee has the resources to bring Trump Jr. before it to answer questions about who paid for his wedding celebrations, while noting that Hunter Biden has previously given sworn testimony to Congress.

Still, bipartisan support for the request does not mean that Trump Jr. has already been subpoenaed or that the Senate has opened a formal investigation. The committee would have to take further action before those steps occur.

For now, the political significance is that Trump Jr.’s finances have moved from a media controversy into a proposed congressional inquiry — with his crypto interests, prediction-market ties and relationship with a Russian businessman now being examined together.

And that could make the questions around the Trump family’s crypto empire much harder to dismiss as merely a political talking point.

data.title: Malicious iOS App FomoPeek Linked To $580K Crypto Theft, SlowMist Says
data.description:
A seemingly legitimate iOS app distributed through Apple’s App Store allegedly turned into a gateway for crypto theft after security researchers discovered malware capable of breaking through Apple’s app sandbox and reaching data belonging to other applications.

‼️ BREAKING: An app on Apple's official App Store was serving iPhone users malware designed to steal crypto wallet keys.

SlowMist and OKX found FomoPeek versions 1.1 and 1.2, distributed Sept 9–17, hid a kernel exploit framework built to escape the iOS sandbox, decrypt the… pic.twitter.com/PISIrQV0KN

— International Cyber Digest (@IntCyberDigest) September 22, 2026

The app, called FomoPeek, has been linked by blockchain security firm SlowMist to an incident involving nearly $580,000 in stolen cryptocurrency. Unlike a conventional crypto phishing attack, the campaign did not require victims to visit a malicious website or open a compromised webpage. Instead, the malicious framework was loaded when the app itself launched.

FomoPeek Exploited iOS to Reach Beyond Its Own App

According to SlowMist, FomoPeek contained two malicious modules capable of exploiting multiple iOS vulnerabilities, gaining elevated privileges and escaping the operating system’s normal application sandbox. That potentially allowed the malware to reach sensitive Keychain data and files belonging to other apps on the device.

The affected versions were released on Sept. 9 and Sept. 12, while FomoPeek version 1.3, released Sept. 17, removed the malicious components. SlowMist said its investigation, conducted with the OKX security team, began after users reported asset theft and researchers found that some victims had previously installed the affected versions.

Mấy ngày trước bên trung rất nhiều các kols lớn share cái app này và nói rằng nó tương tự như fomo app. Nếu ai đăng ký tài khoản mới còn được tặng 5$$-10$$ gì đó.

Đến hôm nay nó đã bị tố giác là 1 app đánh cắp tài sản crypto , rất nhiều người cài app này đã bị… https://t.co/n0EZ5jMy2gpic.twitter.com/06E7R1qAJW

— Eternal  (@Eternals_io) September 19, 2026

The exploit framework contained eight attack methods and declared support for iOS versions ranging from 12.0 to 18.7.2 and 26.0 to 26.1. That broad compatibility made the discovery particularly concerning, because the threat was not limited to a single outdated version of Apple’s operating system.

SlowMist said the framework could also be controlled remotely, allowing a server to direct exploitation and data-collection functions after the application launched.

Crypto Wallets and Apple Notes Were Among the Targets

The researchers found a server configuration listing 19 wallet and note-taking applications as potential targets. Those included MetaMask, Trust Wallet, SafePal, OKX Wallet and Apple Notes, putting both cryptocurrency credentials and potentially sensitive personal information within the framework’s reach.

SlowMist confirmed that the malware was capable of collecting application data in a controlled environment, including data from the Apple Notes container. But the researchers stopped short of claiming that every named wallet had its private keys or seed phrases extracted.

You just need one account to earn, trade, and spend.

MetaMask Money Account.

🦊 pic.twitter.com/0uvjI4dfx6

— MetaMask 🦊 (@MetaMask) September 21, 2026

That distinction matters. The investigation demonstrates that FomoPeek had the technical capability to access data from targeted applications, but it does not establish that every wallet listed in the malware’s configuration was compromised or that a seed phrase was stolen from each one.

The on-chain evidence nevertheless points to a substantial theft connected to the campaign. SlowMist identified a primary hacker address that received approximately 579,984 USDT. The address became active on Sept. 15, with funds moving across multiple blockchain networks before being consolidated and routed through additional addresses and services.

⚠️ FomoPeek Linked To $580K Crypto Theft

On-chain tracing links $580K in stolen funds to the FomoPeek iOS app.

The app allegedly used kernel exploits to escape Apple’s sandbox and access sensitive wallet data.

The stolen funds, totaling 579,984.34 USDT, were subsequently moved… pic.twitter.com/YaATMgVKCP

— Emperor.SOL (@Solana_Emperor) September 23, 2026

SlowMist traced portions of the funds toward services including FixedFloat, KuCoin and cce.cash, while continuing to track other transfers through the wider address network.

Uninstalling FomoPeek May Not Be Enough

For users who installed FomoPeek versions 1.1 or 1.2, SlowMist recommends assuming that potentially exposed wallet credentials are compromised. The security firm advises affected users to create a new wallet on an unaffected device and move their assets rather than relying on simply deleting the application.

The reason is that removing the malware does not necessarily undo what it may already have accessed. If an attacker successfully exploited the device and copied sensitive information away from it, that information remains outside the victim’s control even after the malicious application is removed.

我日，你们推广 FomoPeek 一个人头 50U ？ pic.twitter.com/TtvlK9cTQc

— RK_Rocky (@RK_Bitcoin) September 19, 2026

SlowMist specifically warned that enabling Lockdown Mode or uninstalling the application after a successful compromise cannot recover data that has already been exfiltrated.

The incident highlights a particularly uncomfortable problem for crypto users: the attack surface may not always be a suspicious link, a fake wallet website or a compromised browser. In this case, researchers say the threat came through an application distributed via Apple’s own App Store and relied on vulnerabilities inside the operating system to cross the boundary between apps.

data.title: Jeff Yan Warned Bitget Could Become the Next FTX. Then Hyperliquid Faced Its Own FTX Moment
data.description:
The FTX Warning That Started a Crypto Exchange Feud

In April 2023, just one day after venture firm Dragonfly announced a $10 million investment in crypto exchange Bitget, Jeff Yan issued a warning that would later come back to haunt both sides of the dispute.

Jeff predicted the Bitget situation back in 2023.

The Hyperliquid founder had already warned the community about potential risks, saying that Bitget could become the next FTX.

Ignoring the guy who built the antidote to FTX was a mistake.

Ironically, Bitget CEO tried so hard to… https://t.co/qGGBi0PgvWpic.twitter.com/jxFExkee1j

— Maven.HL (@MavenHL) September 24, 2026

Yan, then known for founding high-frequency trading firm Chameleon Trading and later becoming a co-founder of decentralized derivatives exchange Hyperliquid, publicly claimed that Bitget “may become the next FTX.” His argument was because the exchange faced problems. He questioned whether its handling of customer orders gave the platform an advantage over the traders using it.

Bitget has suspended withdrawals following a massive 351.6 million dollar security breach involving its hot wallets. CEO Gracy Chen confirms the exchange is utilizing its 464 million dollar protection fund to cover user losses while investigations continue. Azat TV pic.twitter.com/eK8fJXJbBj

— Azat TV (@azattelevision) September 25, 2026

Yan said he respected Dragonfly for investing during a bear market, but argued that investors had a responsibility to scrutinize exchanges before giving them more capital and allowing them to expand. His warning invoked the collapse of FTX and LUNA, two disasters that had already demonstrated how quickly failures at major crypto projects could spread through the industry.

His accusations centered on something traders rarely see directly: what happens to an order after a customer clicks “buy” or “sell.”

Yan Accused Bitget of Taking the Other Side of Its Customers

Yan said his concerns came from his own experience trading on Bitget. About six months before his public warning, he said his high-frequency trading team noticed what he described as a “dishonest” matching engine.

According to Yan, his orders could sit at the best bid or ask while trades appeared to execute at worse prices without his orders being filled. He argued that the phenomenon was visible through Bitget’s trading interface and said his firm stopped trading on the exchange after encountering it.

BÀI CŨ CỦA CEO HYPERLIQUID VỀ BITGET ĐANG BỊ ĐÀO LẠI SAU VỤ HACK 351,6M$.

Từ năm 2023, Jeff Yan từng viết thẳng rằng “Bitget may be the next FTX”, đồng thời cáo buộc cách vận hành matching engine của sàn có vấn đề.

Giờ Bitget vừa xác nhận sự cố hot wallet… pic.twitter.com/hzFc04RlMS

— Piz (@WhalePiz) September 25, 2026

Yan also cited an alleged account from a former Bitget employee concerning the exchange’s treatment of retail order flow. The claim was that Bitget used a B-booking model for some retail trades, in which an internal trading operation could take the opposite side of customer positions rather than sending those orders into an external market.

That distinction is important because it changes the economic relationship between an exchange and its customers. Under a B-book model, a platform acting as the counterparty can potentially profit when customers lose, whereas an exchange that simply matches customers with outside liquidity providers generally earns fees regardless of which side wins.

Yan argued that retail traders, particularly those participating in copy trading, represented valuable order flow that could be profitable to take the other side of. He accused Bitget of retaining that flow rather than relying more heavily on external market makers.

Bitget did not accept Yan’s characterization. Gracy Chen, who was then the exchange’s managing director and later became its CEO, said Bitget’s matching engine worked like those of other major exchanges, albeit potentially with differences in efficiency.

gracy chen wished death to hyperliquid

sorry not sorry https://t.co/5SdgClsN3epic.twitter.com/HFeyq2PaiG

— hrithik ( 히리틱 ) (@hrithikk) September 24, 2026

Yan responded that the dispute extended beyond the technical operation of the matching engine. He questioned whether Bitget was effectively “betting against customers” and also raised allegations that profitable traders had their APIs or VIP levels restricted. Those claims were not specifically resolved in the public exchange between the two sides.

Then the FTX Accusation Came Back Around

At the time, Yan’s warning was directed squarely at Bitget. But two years later, the exchange founded by Yan became the subject of its own controversy — and Bitget was suddenly the one raising the FTX comparison.

On March 26, 2025, the JELLY token surged roughly 230% within an hour on Hyperliquid, leaving the platform’s market-making vault, HLP, facing a large floating loss. The losses were reported at around $10.6 million, with potential exposure at one point estimated at more than $240 million.

Hyperliquid turned a $10M loss into a $$700K gain after a $$JELLY token manipulation. But the move sparked debate over centralization.

What do you think? Watch the full video! 👇 pic.twitter.com/81l1acsPVN

— DEXTools (@DEXToolsApp) March 26, 2025

Hyperliquid responded by delisting JELLY and forcibly settling affected positions. The decision itself became controversial because critics questioned the platform’s authority to intervene in a market after positions had already been established, while Hyperliquid defended the action as necessary to protect the system and its users.

The dispute opened the door for Bitget to turn Yan’s old accusation back on him. By then CEO of Bitget, Gracy Chen criticized Hyperliquid, describing it as resembling “an offshore centralized exchange without KYC and anti-money laundering” and warning that it was heading toward “FTX 2.0.”

The exchange feud had effectively come full circle. Yan had once questioned whether Bitget’s structure gave it too much power over customers. Years later, Bitget was questioning whether Hyperliquid’s decentralized structure gave it too much discretion when a market threatened the platform itself.

Two Exchanges, Two Models and the Same Trust Problem

The argument ultimately reaches beyond the personal dispute between Yan and Chen. It touches one of crypto’s oldest questions: what should an exchange be allowed to do when its interests collide with those of its traders?

Centralized exchanges have historically faced scrutiny over custody, market making, order execution and conflicts of interest. Decentralized derivatives platforms attempt to solve some of those problems through transparent, on-chain infrastructure, but the JELLY episode demonstrated that decentralization does not eliminate difficult decisions when markets become disorderly.

🚨HYPERLIQUID IS PRINTING THE MOST CASH IN CRYPTO!

hyperliquid:native led 2026 onchain revenue through Sept. 15 with $429 million, more than the next two names combined, per CoinGecko.https://t.co/aLQAFhGjzr is second at $322 million.

Real users are paying, and Hyperliquid… pic.twitter.com/iHbTV3qVk0

— Crypto Banter (@crypto_banter) September 20, 2026

Hyperliquid’s growth has also made those questions harder to ignore. By July 13, 2026, its peak open contracts had reached roughly $11 billion, representing about 9% of global perpetual-contract positions. Bitget, meanwhile, processed about $81.7 trillion in derivatives trading volume during 2025, putting it among the largest centralized crypto exchanges by that measure.

The numbers show why the debate matters. These are no longer small experimental platforms where a technical dispute affects only a handful of traders. Both exchanges now operate at a scale where decisions about order flow, market making, liquidations and emergency intervention can affect billions of dollars in positions.

Yan once warned that the crypto industry should be careful about giving exchanges more capital before understanding how they operate behind the scenes. Years later, Hyperliquid faced a different version of the same fundamental question: when an exchange has to choose between protecting its system and preserving the positions of its traders, who ultimately gets to decide what is fair?

The answer may determine whether crypto exchanges can escape the trust failures that helped define the industry’s previous era — regardless of whether the exchange calls itself centralized or decentralized.

data.title: DeepSeek and Kimi Allegedly Leak Confidential Security Information to Claude....Now The Chinese Government Is Demanding For Answer
data.description:
Chinese AI Giants Face a Data-Sovereignty Question

Chinese authorities are investigating DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, the company behind Kimi, after Anthropic accused the two AI firms of secretly routing large volumes of requests through its Claude models. The allegations go beyond a battle over who is copying whose AI: they raise a more uncomfortable question about where users’ data goes when they interact with a chatbot.

China’s Cyberspace Administration has narrowed its scrutiny to DeepSeek and Moonshot after initially summoning the seven Chinese companies named in Anthropic’s September report, according to news reports. The investigation is examining whether sensitive information, including data connected to Chinese government, police, military and corporate systems, was transmitted to US-based AI infrastructure through Claude.

🚨 Kimi・DeepSeekに調査報道

中国当局が、KimiとDeepSeekの“機密漏洩疑惑”を調べているとの報道。

ポイントはここ👇
・Kimiが中国軍関係者の依頼をClaudeに転送した疑惑
・DeepSeekがロシア政府系機関の依頼をClaudeに転送した疑惑
・当局は両社幹部に聞き取りを実施中… pic.twitter.com/VJXdbthltl

— しょー/AIの神 (@god_of_ai7) September 24, 2026

The allegations are particularly striking because Anthropic says Moonshot did not merely use Claude as a research tool. In one case, nearly 300,000 real customer requests were allegedly forwarded to Claude over 10 days, with most routed to Anthropic’s Opus model, before Claude’s responses were presented to users as part of their Kimi experience. Moonshot allegedly used a network of 5,380 fraudulent accounts to access Claude, because Anthropic restricts access to its services from inside China.

🚨 Kimi・DeepSeekに調査報道

中国当局が、KimiとDeepSeekの“機密漏洩疑惑”を調べているとの報道。

ポイントはここ👇
・Kimiが中国軍関係者の依頼をClaudeに転送した疑惑
・DeepSeekがロシア政府系機関の依頼をClaudeに転送した疑惑
・当局は両社幹部に聞き取りを実施中… pic.twitter.com/VJXdbthltl

— しょー/AIの神 (@god_of_ai7) September 24, 2026

That creates a very different kind of AI risk. A user asking Kimi to analyze sensitive information may believe the request is staying within Kimi’s ecosystem, while Anthropic alleges that at least some requests were instead sent to Claude and that Moonshot saved portions of those exchanges for use in training its own systems.

The Hidden Pipeline Behind the AI Race

The alleged data flow sits inside a broader fight over AI distillation, a technique in which developers use the outputs of a stronger model to improve another system.

Distillation itself is not inherently illicit. AI companies routinely use model outputs to create smaller, cheaper or specialized systems. Anthropic says the problem in these cases was the alleged use of fraudulent accounts, proxy networks and other methods to circumvent usage restrictions and extract capabilities from Claude at industrial scale. Anthropic has previously accused DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax of generating more than 16 million exchanges through roughly 24,000 fraudulent accounts.

Anthropic has alleged that Chinese entities are targeting its AI models to copy their capabilities — using a technique called distillation. Here's a look at the geopolitical row over AI competition and whether China is pulling ahead https://t.co/clEaie8s7ipic.twitter.com/EHnFysMXTd

— Reuters (@Reuters) September 23, 2026

Anthropic’s September investigation expanded those allegations dramatically. It says Moonshot generated more than 23 million exchanges between May and July, while DeepSeek generated more than 12.1 million exchanges during a 14-day period in July. The figures describe exchanges with Claude and should not automatically be interpreted as 35 million ordinary end-user conversations; they are measurements reported by Anthropic as part of its investigation.

The alleged use of Claude also appears to have gone beyond simply obtaining polished answers. Anthropic says Moonshot built systems to extract Claude’s reasoning-related data from saved exchanges and use it to train its own models.

In one example cited by Anthropic, a Kimi user supplied surveillance footage involving hundreds of cameras in Chengdu, including cameras near PLA facilities and other sensitive institutions. Another example involved an engineer at a Chinese state-owned enterprise who allegedly exposed internal code and live credentials while using Kimi.

We're publishing our most detailed threat intelligence report to date.

It covers how people tried to misuse Claude—for cyberattacks, influence operations, surveillance, biology, and building weapons—and how we found and stopped them.

We disrupted every operation in the report,…

— Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) September 10, 2026

That distinction matters. The most consequential question is no longer simply whether one AI company learned from another. It is whether sensitive information entered one AI ecosystem and emerged inside another without the person submitting it fully understanding what was happening.

The AI Data Pipeline Is Becoming a Geopolitical Problem

The investigation arrives at a particularly sensitive moment for the global AI race. DeepSeek is scheduled to brief the UN Security Council on AI risks, while US and Chinese officials are also discussing AI safety and crisis communication ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.

For Moonshot, the timing is even more complicated because the company is preparing for a major financial milestone. Reuters reported that Moonshot confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO in September, with sources saying it is targeting roughly $3 billion in proceeds and a valuation of about $50 billion. Any regulatory scrutiny could therefore become an additional issue for investors as the Kimi developer prepares for a potential public listing.

US President Donald Trump said that he and Chinese President Xi Jinping had a ‘great meeting’ after the two leaders met at the White House. Trump made the comments to reporters before the two boarded the Marine One helicopter for a brief tour https://t.co/Bn78zyHd0Mpic.twitter.com/jgzaZ0e13P

— Reuters (@Reuters) September 25, 2026

Anthropic, meanwhile, says it plans to tighten controls around how its APIs can be accessed. The company has argued that fraudulent accounts and proxy networks allow competitors to bypass geographic and usage restrictions while extracting capabilities that would otherwise take years and enormous resources to develop independently.

But the controversy exposes a problem that reaches beyond Anthropic, DeepSeek or Moonshot. As AI models become interconnected, the boundary between “your AI assistant” and “someone else’s AI infrastructure” can become increasingly difficult for users to see.

A Chinese user may believe they are sending information to a Chinese AI company. A US AI company may ultimately process part of that request. And regulators in both countries may have very different ideas about whether that data is allowed to cross the border in the first place.

Jensen Huang says the AI labs are not asking for new regulation but to be relieved of the laws that already govern them

That makes the DeepSeek and Moonshot investigation about more than alleged model distillation. It is a warning that the next AI battle may not be fought only over who builds the smartest model, but over who controls the data flowing between them.

As AI companies increasingly rely on one another’s models, APIs and infrastructure, the question facing users is becoming harder to ignore: when you send a query to an AI, do you actually know who is receiving it?
